output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly frontal-executive profile. Executive function is severely impaired across multiple measures: Trail Making B discontinued, WCST 1/6 categories completed, Stroop z = −2.4, and Go/No-Go 40% commission errors. Verbal fluency is markedly impaired for both phonemic (FAS 14 total) and semantic (animals 9/min) categories. Episodic memory is also impaired (CVLT-3 long delay 3/16). Clock drawing is mildly impaired (7/10). Visuoconstructive skill and confrontation naming are relatively preserved. Informant behavioral rating (Frontal Behavioral Inventory 32/72) indicates significant behavioral dyscontrol. Profile is consistent with a frontal-executive syndrome with concurrent episodic memory impairment

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)

accepted: Frontal (behavioral/dysexecutive) variant of early-onset Alzheimer's disease

differential.key_features: Clinically the closest mimic — disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, dietary changes; distinguished by amyloid PET (positive in frontal AD, negative in bvFTD) and FDG-PET pattern (temporoparietal hypometabolism in AD vs frontotemporal in FTD)

differential.diagnosis: Primary psychiatric disorder (late-onset mood or personality disorder)
differential.key_features: Behavioral changes at this age can be mistaken for primary psychiatry; objective neuropsychological deficits, progressive course, and biomarker positivity differentiate frontal AD from a psychiatric diagnosis
Lack of motor features (asymmetric rigidity, alien limb, oculomotor abnormalities, postural instability) argues against these atypical parkinsonian syndromes
Excluded by absence of focal vascular lesions on MRI
Excluded by history and review of medications; no exposure to neurotoxic agents or substance use

key_clinical_evidence: Definite hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI with a multi-domain amnestic cognitive profile is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of probable AD by NIA-AA 2011 criteria
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
Frontal variant AD is the closest mimic of bvFTD; amyloid PET positivity differentiates AD from FTD pathology
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease

clinical_assessment.impression: Cognitive impairment documented on a validated bedside instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile, and delayed recall that does not recover with cueing — a storage rather than a retrieval deficit, which is the pattern of Alzheimer pathology. The informant history and the loss of instrumental independence establish decline from a previous level and place the syndrome at the dementia rather than the mild threshold. This assessment is the step that makes the syndrome measurable; imaging and biomarkers then attribute it.

metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Differentiating frontal variant AD from behavioral variant FTD in a patient with frontal-predominant behavioral and executive deficits, complicated by a family history suggestive of FTD
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Required core: structured assessment with informant and functional staging, validated neuropsychological testing, the reviewed cognitive laboratory panel, and brain MRI. Biomarker route: optional amyloid PET, with no duplicate CSF/PET confirmation. Case-specific additions: optional FDG-PET for the atypical subtype question; optional counselled APP/PSEN1/PSEN2 testing.
metadata.educational_value: Teaches recognition of frontal variant AD as an atypical AD presentation that mimics bvFTD, and the critical role of AD biomarkers in differentiating these conditions
key_educational_points: Frontal variant AD can be clinically indistinguishable from bvFTD based on behavioral symptoms alone
Concurrent episodic memory impairment in a behavioral/dysexecutive presentation should raise suspicion for AD rather than pure FTD
FDG-PET showing posterior temporoparietal involvement in addition to frontal hypometabolism favors AD over FTD
Family history of behavioral dementia does not confirm FTD — familial AD can present with frontal symptoms
Negative FTD gene panel (MAPT, GRN, C9orf72) helps exclude genetic FTD but does not rule out sporadic bvFTD
Genetic testing is optional and requires pre-test counselling; APOE is not used to diagnose Alzheimer disease
This case exposes optional amyloid PET as its only biomarker route; conclusive CSF biomarkers and amyloid PET must not be ordered together

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sofia Reyes is a 58-year-old right-handed bank branch manager who is referred to the neurology outpatient clinic by her primary care physician for evaluation of progressive behavioral changes and cognitive decline over the past 18 months. Her husband, who accompanies her, provides the majority of the history as the patient tends to minimize and joke about her difficulties. Approximately 18 months ago, her husband first noticed subtle changes in her personality. She began making inappropriate comments to colleagues and customers at the bank, including remarking on a customer's weight and making off-color jokes during staff meetings — behavior completely out of character for someone who had been known for her professionalism and interpersonal skills. Over the following months, she became increasingly apathetic, losing interest in activities she previously enjoyed including running, cooking, and socializing with friends. She has had progressive difficulty with organizational tasks at work — she was previously meticulous with documentation and compliance protocols, but began making errors in loan approvals, forgot to file regulatory reports, and could not manage multiple tasks simultaneously. Her judgment deteriorated — she made several impulsive online purchases totaling over $8,000 in a single month, bought items she already owned, and signed up for multiple streaming subscriptions she never used. After receiving formal complaints from three customers and two staff members about her inappropriate remarks, she was placed on medical leave 4 months ago. She was seen by a psychiatrist who diagnosed depression and tried sertraline 100 mg daily for 8 weeks, then switched to venlafaxine 150 mg for 6 weeks — neither improved her behavioral symptoms, and the language difficulties continued to progress. Importantly, her husband reports that in addition to the behavioral changes, she has developed concurrent memory problems. She frequently forgets conversations from earlier in the day, repeats questions multiple times, forgets appointments despite using calendar reminders, and recently forgot that her daughter had visited the previous weekend. She also has difficulty learning new information — she could not figure out how to use a new coffee maker despite repeated instruction. She has not gotten lost but has had difficulty planning meals and following recipes she previously made from memory. She denies visual hallucinations, paranoid ideation, or delusional thinking. Sleep is unremarkable. There is no history of head trauma, seizures, or substance abuse. Her father's history of behavioral dementia beginning at age 70 is noted.
